title: The Landfall of Patagonia's dry side
premise: Paloma Dunmore, a storm chaser drowning in debt to the Ferro brothers—cheerful, patient, dangerous lenders—takes a salvage contract to find a vanished government survey team on Patagonia's arid eastern steppe. He finds one survivor, Dr. Ines Cabral, who carries data proving the government knew about a poisoned aquifer years ago and buried it; her loyalty is to her dead teammates' memory, his is to the money that keeps his family safe. As the Ferros' deadline closes and a second, dirtier crew hunts the same evidence, Paloma must choose between delivering Ines and the drives to the men who own him or exposing a truth that will ruin him. In the end he burns his contract, smuggles the data out through a storm only he can read, and pays his debt with the one currency the Ferros never expected: the truth about what they were helping bury.
about_author: Rosalind Almeida spent a decade guiding overland expeditions across southern Argentina before turning to fiction, and her prose carries the dust of that country in every line. She writes from a farmhouse outside Puerto Madryn, where she keeps unreliable weather instruments and even less reliable dogs.

chapters.title: The Debt of Good Weather
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Chasing a dying storm across the steppe for paying clients, he returns to find the Ferro brothers waiting in his rented garage, smiling, resetting the terms of his debt. The beat is dread dressed as charm: we learn exactly how trapped he is, and how good he is at reading weather no one else can.

chapters.title: A Contract Written in Pencil
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A government fixer offers him salvage work: locate the vanished Río Deseado survey team, recover their gear, tell no one. The pay clears his debt twice over. Emotional beat: temptation—he knows a job this easy-paying is never easy, but poverty argues louder than instinct.

chapters.title: Where the Tracks Stop
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, opening the expedition. He follows the team's route north along the dry side, finding an orderly camp abandoned mid-meal: kettles warm, radios intact, no tracks leaving. The beat is quiet wrongness—the wilderness has hidden something, and it wants him to know it.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Wouldn't Be Dead
chapters.summary: Ines Cabral's POV. We flash back eleven days: the survey team drilling core samples, Ines finding readings that don't match any filed report, and her team leader ordering the data sealed. The beat is dawning betrayal—she realizes the disappearance was arranged before they ever left.

chapters.title: One Survivor, No Story
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. He finds Ines half-buried in a guanaco carcass pit, alive by discipline alone. She gives him a name, a cover story, and nothing true. Beat: two liars taking each other's measure, each deciding the other might be useful.

chapters.title: What the Cores Said
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, continued flashback. The aquifer beneath the survey grid is laced with mining runoff, and the ministry signed off on concealment two years ago. Her teammate Tomás hid duplicate drives in the drill casings. Beat: grief hardening into purpose—she will bring the data out or die beside it.

chapters.title: The Second Crew
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. At a fuel stop he recognizes a truck: the Ferros have subcontracted a cleanup crew to make sure nothing comes back from the steppe. Beat: cold clarity—the salvage job was always a search-and-destroy, and he was hired as the bloodhound.

chapters.title: Radio Silence
chapters.summary: Alternating short sections, Paloma and Ines. They agree on a fragile alliance: she'll lead him to the buried drives if he gets her to a journalist in Comodoro Rivadavia instead of the ministry. Beat: loyalty vs. truth made explicit between them, neither trusting, both committing.

chapters.title: Tomás's Casing
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Digging up the drill site at night, they recover one drive—and find Tomás's body, buried shallow, hands still holding a second casing marker. Beat: the cost becomes physical; Ines breaks, and Paloma sees the mission is now hers, not the government's.

chapters.title: The Ferro Brothers Send Regards
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A satellite call: the Ferros know what he's carrying and offer to forgive everything if he delivers drive and woman to their contact. Beat: temptation sharpened into threat—they remind him, gently, where his sister lives.

chapters.title: Dust Devil Country
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. A cross-country run south, pursued, as Ines learns who Paloma owes and what he stands to lose. Beat: love beginning against duty—she starts seeing the man inside the mercenary, and hates herself a little for it.

chapters.title: The Estancia at Bajo Caracoles
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. An old guide who once ran with Paloma's father shelters them for a night and refuses payment, saying some debts are paid forward. Beat: warmth and foreshadowing—the old man warns that the cleanup crew doesn't leave witnesses, and that storms on the dry side come fast and lie about their size.

chapters.title: Interrogation of a Ghost
chapters.summary: Antagonist POV (the cleanup chief, Vidal). Vidal interrogates a fuel-station owner and reconstructs their route. Beat: menace without violence—we see how methodical the hunt is, and how little time remains.

chapters.title: The Drive That Lies
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Examining the recovered drive, Paloma discovers it's partially corrupted—or doctored—and realizes Ines may be feeding him a curated truth. Beat: trust fractures; loyalty vs. truth turns inward, each wondering if the other is the trap.

chapters.title: Confession in a Dry Riverbed
chapters.summary: Two-hander scene, both POVs interleaved. Ines admits she held back names of officials to protect a source; Paloma admits the Ferros hold his sister's lease. Beat: full honesty at last, and with it something like love—not tender, but load-bearing.

chapters.title: Ambush at the Pass
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Vidal's crew boxes them in a canyon pass; a running firefight on foot, Ines shot through the shoulder, the drive nearly lost. Beat: survival at raw cost—Paloma wins the escape by doing the thing he swore off: using the storm he can feel building.

chapters.title: The Storm Only He Can Read
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. He deliberately leads them into the path of a massive dust-front he's tracked since dawn, navigating by pressure and instinct while Vidal's trucks lose the light. Beat: competence as catharsis—the wilderness forgives nothing, but tonight it takes his side.

chapters.title: What Vidal Offers
chapters.summary: Vidal's POV, then Paloma's. Cornered at a rail siding, Vidal offers Paloma his sister's safety and total debt forgiveness for the drive. Beat: the climax of temptation—everything he wanted, handed over, if he just hands over Ines too.

chapters.title: Landfall
chapters.summary: Climax, Paloma's POV. He pretends to deal, passes Vidal a decoy drive, and triggers the confrontation as the storm makes landfall; Ines, wounded but standing, records Vidal's admission of the burial order on the surviving device. Beat: choice made—truth over safety, at the moment safety was finally offered.

chapters.title: Settling Accounts
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. He walks into the Ferros' office and gives them not money but leverage: proof their government contact used them as deniable muscle, plus a copy of everything as insurance. Beat: audacity as resolution—the debt dies because he stops being prey.

chapters.title: The Story Breaks
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. From a hospital in Comodoro, she watches the aquifer story detonate across the news; officials fall, Tomás gets his name back. Beat: grief transmuted—victory that tastes like ash, because three friends aren't here to see it.

chapters.title: Weather Coming Fair
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, closing. Months later, broke again but free, he meets Ines at the estancia where the old guide laughs at them both; a new storm builds on the horizon and, for once, he isn't chasing it for money. Beat: earned peace—love without duty attached, and the wilderness, grudgingly, letting them keep it.
